title: Renew, keep or buy: Dana's next car
question: When the lease ends in March, should Dana's family keep and repair the car, renew the lease, buy new, buy used, or go car-free?
summary: Car share is cheapest but fails the school run. Keeping the old car costs least over five years, unless repairs run high. Buying used is the sturdier choice: about $2,500 more than keeping, $11,000 less than leasing, with long warranty cover. The scores are a close call between buying new and buying used.
reading: Start with the list on the left. The scoring table checks the must-haves first, then weighs what matters; try your own weights with Change the weights. The cost view shows what each option really costs month by month; switch the what-ifs on to see how the answer moves. The journey shows what changes in day-to-day life. The notes are from different points of view, each ending in a question.

checked.note: Checked against the lease letter, the garage visit, two dealer offers, insurance quotes, car share prices, a family talk and published figures from AAA, Kelley Blue Book, Edmunds and the EIA.

glossary.real cost: Money spent so far, plus any loan still owed, minus what the car could be sold for.
glossary.buyout: Buying the car you have been leasing, at the price set when the lease began.
glossary.residual: What the leasing company expects the car to be worth at the end of the lease.
glossary.certified: A used car checked by the maker's dealer and sold with extra warranty cover.
glossary.must-have: Something an option has to meet. If it fails, it is out, whatever its score.
glossary.what-if: A change to one assumption, such as petrol prices, to see how the answer moves.
glossary.pre-mortem: Imagining the decision has already gone badly and listing why, before deciding.

notes.title: The monthly number hides the five-year cost
notes.body: At $520 a month the lease looks close to the loan payments, but after five years Dana owns nothing, and signing again in year four costs another $2,500.
notes.recommend: Compare five-year real cost, not monthly payments.
notes.question: Is a lower monthly payment worth about $13,500 more over five years than keeping the car?

notes.title: The used car's loan rate is the soft spot
notes.body: Dealer finance at 9.5% adds about $6,500 of interest over five years. A credit union loan at 7% would save around $1,700.
notes.recommend: Get a loan offer before visiting the dealer.
notes.question: Will Dana get a credit union quote before 1 February?

notes.title: Repairs on a five-year-old car rise
notes.body: The garage expects suspension parts and a battery soon, and bills that grow each year.
notes.recommend: Treat the repair budget as a range, and check the 'repairs run high' what-if.
notes.question: What repair bill in one year would make Dana sell the old car?

notes.title: Certified cover takes the worst risk away
notes.body: The certified warranty covers engine and gearbox to 7 years or 100,000 miles, which is where big bills come from.
notes.recommend: Read what the certified cover excludes before signing.
notes.question: Does the certified cover include the gearbox electronics, or only the mechanical parts?

notes.title: The old car lacks the newer driver aids
notes.body: The 2022 car passed its crash tests, but has no automatic braking at junctions. The 2024 model has most aids; the 2027 has all of them.
notes.question: Is junction braking worth about $6,000 more over five years (new against used)?

notes.title: The school run decides the car share question
notes.body: The car share spot is often empty at 8 a.m., and carrying two child seats each day is not realistic.
notes.recommend: Treat car share as out unless a school bus or a lift share appears.
notes.question: Is there any other way to do the school run that would make car-free possible?

notes.title: Dana's partner wants out of the lease cycle
notes.body: "I want to stop paying for something we never own." Renewing the lease would go against this.
notes.question: Has the partner seen the five-year numbers for leasing against owning?

notes.title: A job change could double the miles
notes.body: If the commute doubles, the lease's 12,000-mile limit would be broken and extra miles charged; owning has no limit, and keeping the old car gets dearer faster.
notes.recommend: Look at the cost view with 'Commute doubles' switched on.
notes.question: How likely is the job change in the next year?

notes.title: 10 minutes, 10 months, 10 years
notes.body: In 10 minutes, a new car feels best. In 10 months, the payment is what Dana notices. In 10 years, only the money saved and the family's safety matter.
notes.question: Which of the three views should carry the most weight for this family?

notes.title: Keeping a car longer is often the lighter choice
notes.body: Building a new car uses a lot of energy and materials; driving an existing car for longer usually uses less overall. Car share would be lighter still if it worked for the school run.
notes.question: Does the environmental view change the ranking for Dana, or only break a tie?

notes.title: A new car loses the most value early
notes.body: Cars lose about 20% of their value in the first year and about 60% over five. Buying a three-year-old car skips the steepest drop.
notes.question: If Dana might sell within three years, is buying new still sensible?

notes.title: Used prices could fall
notes.body: If used prices fall 15%, the used car is worth less when sold, adding about $2,100 to its five-year cost.
notes.question: Does a $2,100 swing change the choice between keeping and buying used?

notes.title: A year later this went badly. Why?
notes.body: Imagine it is March 2028 and the choice was a mistake. Likely reasons: the old car needed a $3,000 repair; the used car had a hidden fault; the job change doubled the miles; we stretched the budget for a new car and felt squeezed.
notes.recommend: Guard against each: a repair limit for the old car, an independent inspection of the used one, and the doubled-miles what-if.
notes.question: Which of these failure reasons worries Dana most, and what would prevent it?

notes.title: Keeping wins on cost, so why not keep?
notes.body: Keeping is cheapest over five years. The reasons not to are safety aids, hassle and the repair risk, which are real but worth naming plainly.
notes.question: Would Dana keep the car if the garage gave a fixed price for the next two years of repairs?
